data.title: Tuafanua Trail
data.shortDescription: Moderate = 2.2mi/3.54km total; 219ft/67m elevation gain; 2-3 hours. The trail leads you via ladders, steps, and ropes to a rocky beach, where you can enjoy the sound of the waves and take in the Western view of Pola Island.

images.altText: Outdoors; landscape view of sandy beach foreground, blue waters, and steep cliffs in background.
images.title: Tuafanua Trail
images.caption: Enjoy the stunning view of Pola Island from a different angle.

data.accessibilityInformation: Due to needing to use ladders, steps, and ropes the viewpoint is not accessible.

data.title: Mount Alava Trail
data.shortDescription: Difficult = 7mi/11.27km total; 1,607ft/490m elevation gain; 4-5 hours. Trail can be steep, slippery, and rocky in places. Stunning panoramic views from the summit. Lush rainforest environment, great for bird and fruit bat watching.

images.altText: Outdoors; person holding binoculars looking out through greenery at blue waters in the distance.
images.title: Mount Alava Trail
images.caption: Well worth a strenuous hike for a stunning view.

data.accessibilityInformation: Due to being steep, slippery, and rocky this trail not considered accessible.
data.longDescription:

data.title: Lower Sauma Ridge Trail
data.shortDescription: Easy = 0.4mi/0.64km total; 232ft/7m elevation gain; 30-45 minutes. A gentle climb to an archaeological site featuring ancient grinding stones, this trail combines history with incredible views of the northeast coastline and the Vai’ava Strait.

images.altText: A row of men seen from behind hiking a narrow trail downward on low stone steps surrounded by trees.
images.title: Lower Sa'uma Trail
images.caption: Hikers on Lower Sa'uma Trail.

data.accessibilityInformation: One scenic overlook (Lower Sauma Ridge) is accessible with assistance. No other pullouts or overlooks have been developed at this time and trails are unimproved, steep, and rugged.
data.timeOfDayDescription: Morning is the best time to hike the trail to avoid intense sun and heat.
data.longDescription:

data.title: Pola Island Trail
data.shortDescription: Easy = 0.1mi/0.16km total; 30ft/9m elevation gain; 15-30 minutes. This short, easy trail leads you to the untouched shores of the South Pacific; delivering big rewards with views of the rugged coastline and Pola Island, a sanctuary for nesting seabirds.

images.altText: Outdoors; group of young adults facing an adult standing next to sign, trail and forest behind.
images.title: Pola Island Trail
images.caption: Enjoy one of the easiest strolls on the island.

data.accessibilityInformation: Even though the easiest trail in terms of elevation and distance, due to uneven surface this trail isn't necessarily accessible.
data.locationDescription: Trailhead for Pola Island Trail; continue from paved road to gravel road until reaching large turnaround, park where able. Road conditions; single lane with passing oppurtunities, rutted and tree roots.
data.longDescription:

data.title: Upper Sauma Ridge Trail
data.shortDescription: Strenuous = 3.2mi/5.15km total; 1,489ft/454m elevation gain; 3-4 hours. Hike a challenging trail through a dense rainforest, surrounded by native trees and birds. Enjoy one of the island’s most beautiful views of Vatia village and Pola Island at the summit.

images.altText: Outdoors; view of water below, mountains behind, framed with lush greenery.
images.title: Upper Sauma View
images.caption: The hike is worth it when you get views like this.

data.accessibilityInformation: The trail is steep and very rocky. Footing is uneven and can be slippery.
data.longDescription:

data.title: Fruit Bat Watching
data.shortDescription: Fruit bats are the only native mammals found in American Samoa. The two species of fruit bat and one insect-eating bat species are harmless to people. They have a wingspan close to three feet. As fruit eaters, fruit bats are excellent and vital pollinators. Plants rely on the fruit bat to spread its seeds through droppings. A colony of fruit bats ensures that the tropical rainforest remains healthy and full of new trees.

images.altText: A fruit bat flies over a tree with other fruit bats in its branches, against a blue sky.
images.title: Fruit bats flying over a tree.
images.caption: A fruit bat flies over a tree with other fruit bats in its branches.

data.longDescription:
Fruit bats are the only native mammals found in American Samoa. The two species of fruit bat and one insect-eating bat species are harmless to people. They have a wingspan close to three feet. 

As fruit eaters, fruit bats are excellent and vital pollinators. Plants rely on the fruit bat to spread its seeds through droppings. A colony of fruit bats ensures that the tropical rainforest remains healthy and full of new trees.

data.title: Snorkeling
data.shortDescription: Each island of American Samoa supports a coral reef ecosystem in its coastal waters. These coral reefs support a variety of marine life typical of tropical Indo-Pacific waters. To date, over 950 species of fish and over 250 species of coral have been documented.

images.altText: A snorkeler floats near the top of the image at the water's surface, with coral in the foreground.
images.title: Snorkeling in Vatia Village.
images.caption: A snorkeler floats over coral.

data.title: Take a boat ride to Aunu'u
data.shortDescription: About one mile southeast of Tutuila’s eastern tip is the volcanic island of ‘Aunu’u, the smallest inhabited island. It can be reached by boat and explored by foot. 'Aunu'u Island is an excellent exposure of a relatively young flow of basalt inter-bedded with layers of tuff. The site also illustrates erosion by wave action and is covered with dense tropical vegetation.

images.altText: A red and silver boat with a blue canopy sits in shallow waters between a beach and a lush island.
images.title: Take a boat ride to Aunu'u.
images.caption: Take a boat ride to Aunu'u and see the island.

data.feeDescription: Fees apply at the site. Check with local boat charter companies.
data.locationDescription: Drive the coast east village of 'Au'asi and take the 'Aunu'u Island ferry. The ferry may stop running mid-day, so make sure you know when your captain will return.
data.longDescription: About one mile southeast of Tutuila’s eastern tip is the volcanic island of ‘Aunu’u, the smallest inhabited island. It can be reached by boat and explored by foot. 'Aunu'u Island is an excellent exposure of a relatively young flow of basalt inter-bedded with layers of tuff. The site also illustrates erosion by wave action and is covered with dense tropical vegetation.
